actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area

documentation.range: This viper ranges from much of Iran (possibly Iraq) and parts of the Arabian Peninsula (United Arab Emirates and Oman) in the east of its range, and through much of South Asia (southern Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh). It is found over much of southern, central and eastern Iran (Latifi 1991). It is present in Turkmenistan, southwest Tajikistan, and southern Uzbekistan (Ananjeva et al. 2006). The species is present throughout Pakistan, exclusive of the Himalayan region (Minton 1966). It has been recorded to at least 1,800 m asl in Pakistan; and from sea level to 2,063 m asl in Iran. In India, it is found throughout the country except West Bengal and Northeast (Whitaker and Captain 2004), and reaches the lower Himalayan region (L. Borkin pers. comm. 2016).
documentation.population: It is common throughout its range. Minton (1966) reports that it is abundant in Pakistan. It is a very common species in southern Iran (S. Shafiei Bafti and T. Papenfuss pers. comm. 2008), and within its Central Asian range (L. Borkin pers. comm. 2016). It is generally a common species in India.
documentation.habitats: This adaptable species is found in both sandy and rocky desert areas with soft, sandy and alluvial soils, with vegetation ranging from sparse dry scrub to moderately dense grassland (Minton 1966, Latifi 1991). In the northern Western Ghats this species is found in semi-evergreen forests on plateaux. Animals have been reported from mangroves in eastern and western India. Mainly nocturnal, will bask in the morning sun (Whitaker and Captain 2004). Populations have also been recorded from clay deserts (G. Nilson pers. comm. 2008). Individuals may be found under rocks and among other ground cover, but can be encountered in small bushes (up to 3 m high). The species is ovoviviparous; females give birth to up to 23 young (Latifi 1991). It may locally migrate, aestivate or hibernate, as in India as many as 2,000 individuals were recorded in one week in Ratnagiri district of Maharashtra in July, but not a single snake was detected in December (Whitaker and Captain 2004).
documentation.threats: There appear to be no major threats to this species as a whole. In some areas (such as Goa, India) habitat loss through conversion of plateau areas for commercial use is considered to be a threat. In parts of its range, populations might be locally impacted by over-collection for their use in anti-venom production; this remains ongoing at least in Uzbekistan (D. Nuridjanov pers. comm. 2016), although rates of collection have fallen since Soviet times (K. Milto pers. comm. 2016). Animals are often killed on sight by villagers.
documentation.measures: This species is present in many protected areas. Other than general research activities, no direct conservation measures are currently needed for this species as a whole.
documentation.use_trade: Little is known about general use and trade of this species. However, in some places in its range this species is collected for venom extraction.
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, presumed large population, it occurs in a number of protected areas, and because it is unlikely to be declining fast enough to qualify for listing in a more threatened category.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Echis carinatus was described by Schneider in 1801 as Pseudoboa carinata based on the drawings of the species by Dr. Patrick Russell published in 1796 (Smith 1943). Records of this species from Middle Asia and northern Afghanistan were until recently considered to represent the distinct species Echis multisquamatus. Molecular evidence suggests that E. multisquamatus warrants recognition as a subspecies of E. carinatus (Pook et al. 2009) and that scheme is followed here. E. sochureki is recognized as a distinct species from E. carinatus by some authorities.
